messages.author: b5aef0648e455158
messages.subject: Pinning a parameter to zero.
parts:
For identifiability in an IRT model, I need to pin one parameter to zero, as suggested in page 122 "Pinning Parameters" of the Stan Reference 2.4.0.  I have this working with the code below along the lines suggestion in section 7.2, but I want to check to see if this is the most efficient and/or elegant way to do it, because it seems ugly to me.  Do I really have to create an entirely new parameter vector equal to the old one in every way except at one index?  I feel like I must be doing something wrong.    

For reference, "ctrl" and "pd" are two group labels (Control and Parkinson's Disease).  

data {
        int<lower=0,upper=40> n_questions; // number of questions
        int<lower=0> n_subjects; // number of subjects
        int<lower=0> n_control; // number of subjects who are controls
        int<lower=0,upper=1> correct[n_subjects,n_questions]; // 1 if response is correct, 0 if not
        real sigma_g; // sd of subject group means.  
        real sigma_s; // sd within subject groups.  
        real sigma_q; // sd of question difficulty.  
    }
    parameters {
        real r_ctrl_mean; // Mean subject rating for controls.  
        real r_pd_mean; // Mean subject rating for PD.  
        real r_subject[n_subjects]; // Subject skill ratings.  
        vector[n_questions] r_q2; // The unpinned version of the question difficulty ratings.  
    }
    transformed parameters {
        vector[n_questions] r_q; // The pinned version of the question difficulty ratings.  
        r_q[1] <- 0.0; // Pin first question difficulty to zero to avoid collinearity.  
        for (i in 2:n_questions) {
            r_q[i] <- r_q2[i];
        }
    }
    model {
        r_ctrl_mean ~ normal(0, sigma_g);
        r_pd_mean ~ normal(0, sigma_g);
        for (i in 1:n_subjects) {
            if (i <= n_control)
                r_subject[i] ~ normal(r_ctrl_mean,sigma_s);
            else
                r_subject[i] ~ normal(r_pd_mean,sigma_s);
            }
        r_q2 ~ normal(0, sigma_q);
        for (i in 1:n_subjects) {
            for (q in 1:n_questions) {
                correct[i][q] ~ bernoulli_logit(r_subject[i]-r_q[q]);
            }
        }
    }

messages.subject: Re: Pinning a parameter to zero.

On Monday, October 13, 2014 4:28:17 PM UTC-4, Rick Gerkin wrote:
Do I really have to create an entirely new parameter vector equal to the old one in every way except at one index?  I feel like I must be doing something wrong.

Not wrong, although you could put it into the model block to avoid having duplicate output. It is somewhat ugly but assignments are executed really fast.

Ben

For reference, "ctrl" and "pd" are two group labels (Control and Parkinson's Disease).  

data {
        int<lower=0,upper=40> n_questions; // number of questions
        int<lower=0> n_subjects; // number of subjects
        int<lower=0> n_control; // number of subjects who are controls
        int<lower=0,upper=1> correct[n_subjects,n_questions]; // 1 if response is correct, 0 if not
        real sigma_g; // sd of subject group means.  
        real sigma_s; // sd within subject groups.  
        real sigma_q; // sd of question difficulty.  
    }
    parameters {
        real r_ctrl_mean; // Mean subject rating for controls.  
        real r_pd_mean; // Mean subject rating for PD.  
        real r_subject[n_subjects]; // Subject skill ratings.  
        vector[n_questions] r_q2; // The unpinned version of the question difficulty ratings.  
    }
    transformed parameters {
        vector[n_questions] r_q; // The pinned version of the question difficulty ratings.  
        r_q[1] <- 0.0; // Pin first question difficulty to zero to avoid collinearity.  
        for (i in 2:n_questions) {
            r_q[i] <- r_q2[i];
        }
    }
    model {
        r_ctrl_mean ~ normal(0, sigma_g);
        r_pd_mean ~ normal(0, sigma_g);
        for (i in 1:n_subjects) {
            if (i <= n_control)
                r_subject[i] ~ normal(r_ctrl_mean,sigma_s);
            else
                r_subject[i] ~ normal(r_pd_mean,sigma_s);
            }
        r_q2 ~ normal(0, sigma_q);
        for (i in 1:n_subjects) {
            for (q in 1:n_questions) {
                correct[i][q] ~ bernoulli_logit(r_subject[i]-r_q[q]);
            }
        }
    }

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Pinning a parameter to zero.
parts:
The other alternative is to crank down one of the priors (ability
or difficulty) to a normal(0,1) prior so that it controls both
scale and location.

And you only need to put everything together into a single
vector if you need to access it as a single vector. Even so,
as Ben points out, assignment's very fast in Stan relative to
anything introducing partial derivatives to propagate.

I'd also suggest some other changes, mostly for clarity:

> r_pd_mean ~ normal(0, sigma_g);
> for (i in 1:n_subjects) {
> if (i <= n_control)
> r_subject[i] ~ normal(r_ctrl_mean,sigma_s);
> else
> r_subject[i] ~ normal(r_pd_mean,sigma_s);
> }

I find loops like this easier to understand as:

for (i in 1:n_control)
r_subject[i] ~ normal(r_ctrl_mean, sigma_s);
for (i in (n_control+1):n_subjects)
r_subject[i] ~ normal(r_pd_mean, sigma_s);

It's also a bit more efficient, but probably not noticeably so because
there's no change in derivative calculations, just more tests.

It's then easy to see how to reduce it to one-liners involving
slicing the vectors:

head(r_subject, n_control) ~ normal(r_ctrl_mean, sigma_s);

tail(r_subject, n_subjects - n_control) ~ normal(r_pd_mean, sigma_s);

The vectorized version should be faster, but you may decide the
clarity of the first approach is worth the speed hit.

The final inner loop

can also be expressed using vectors as:

correct[i] ~ bernoulli_logit(r_subject[i] - r_q);

That might speed things up a bit. You'll have to change the declarations
from one-dimensional arrays to vectors to support the vector arithmetic
and slicing.

- Bob

messages.author: 2a7f346506a3e9ff
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Pinning a parameter to zero.
parts:
Also, you shouldn't include the pinned value in the parameter block.  E.G., in the parameter block you should have:

vector[n_questions-1] r_q2;

and in the transformed parameter block:

r_q[i] <- r_q2[i-1];
}

This is an extra parameter which you're never using but which could slow sampling down.

Cheers,
Marcus
